title: Shuttle Seats Never Overbooked
statement:
A shuttle with capacity seats drives along one road in one direction, passing kilometre marks 0, 1, 2, and so on. It never turns back.

Each booking trips[i] = [riders, from, to] means riders people board at mark from and leave at mark to. At any mark, people leave before new people board, so a group leaving at mark 5 frees its seats for a group boarding at mark 5.

Return true if every booking can be served without the number of people on board ever going above capacity, and false otherwise.

examples.why: Between marks 2 and 4 both groups are on board: 3 + 2 = 5 people, one more than the seats.
The first group leaves at mark 4 just as the second boards. The two never overlap.
The bookings are not sorted. The busiest stretch is 0–2 with 4 riders, or 5–8 with 3.

hints: The load only changes at marks where someone boards or leaves. Can you record just those changes?
Think of each booking as +riders at mark from and −riders at mark to.
Put those changes in an array indexed by mark, then sweep left to right keeping a running total. If it ever exceeds capacity, return false.

explain.intuition:
Checking every mark against every booking is slow. Instead, notice that a booking only matters at two moments: it adds riders at from and removes them at to. Write those two changes into a difference array indexed by mark. A running sum over that array then gives the exact number of people on board after each mark.

The "leave before board" rule falls out for free. At a shared mark, the −riders and +riders land in the same slot and cancel before you compare with capacity. It is the same idea as counting concurrent users from login and logout events: the number online only changes at events.
steps: Create delta, an array of zeros covering marks 0 to the largest to.
For each booking, do delta[from] += riders and delta[to] −= riders.
Sweep marks left to right with load += delta[m].
If load > capacity at any mark, return false. Otherwise return true.
pitfalls: Treating to as still on board, which double counts at handoff marks. In example 2 the seats are freed at mark 4.
Sorting the events by mark but putting boardings before leavings at the same mark. That reports overload that never happens.
Assuming the bookings are sorted by from. They are not.

complexity.time: O(n + M) where M is the largest mark

solutions.title: Check every mark
solutions.idea: For each mark, add up the riders of all bookings that cover it.

solutions.title: Sorted events
solutions.idea: Turn bookings into (mark, change) events, sort them with leavings first at equal marks, and sweep.

solutions.title: Difference array
solutions.idea: Record +riders at each start and −riders at each end, then take a running sum over the marks.

followups: The marks go up to 10⁹. Which of the solutions still works, and why?
Instead of true/false, return the smallest capacity that serves every booking.
